title: 8. I/O, Redirection & Pipelines
content:
# 8. I/O, Redirection & Pipelines

Unix tools become powerful because programs communicate through streams.

## The three standard streams

```text
0 stdin
1 stdout
2 stderr
```

## Redirect stdout

```bash
ls -la > listing.txt
```

`>` replaces the destination file.

Append instead:

```bash
printf '%s\n' "another line" >> listing.txt
```

## Redirect stderr

```bash
ls /does-not-exist 2> errors.txt
```

Combine stdout and stderr:

```bash
command > all.log 2>&1
```

In Bash, this is also common:

```bash
command &> all.log
```

The first form is more explicit and has broader POSIX-shell relevance.

## Read stdin

```bash
wc -l < listing.txt
```

A program does not need to know the input came from a file.

## Pipes

```bash
journalctl -b | grep -i error
```

Pipeline composition is the core Unix pattern:

```text
produce -> transform -> filter -> summarize
```

## tee

`tee` writes to a file while continuing the pipeline:

```bash
command | tee output.txt
```

## Pipeline status

In Bash:

```bash
set -o pipefail
```

Without `pipefail`, a pipeline's status is normally the status of its last command, which can hide an earlier failure.

## Here documents

```bash
cat <<'EOF'
server {
    listen 8080;
}
EOF
```

Quoting the delimiter prevents parameter and command expansion inside the document.

## Here strings

Bash provides:

```bash
grep 'ERROR' <<< "$text"
```

This is convenient but not POSIX shell syntax.

## Practice

Build a pipeline that:

1. lists files;
2. filters for `.log`;
3. sorts by name;
4. saves the result;
5. displays the result at the same time.

Then deliberately introduce an error and observe how `pipefail` changes the result.
